title: Capital Gains & Tax Harvesting on Equity
tagline: When you sell an investment for a profit, the government wants a share. STCG vs LTCG on equity after the 2024 overhaul, and the legal trick — tax harvesting — that pockets ₹1.25 lakh of gains tax-free every year.
summary: STCG vs LTCG on equity (current rules), the ₹1.25 lakh exemption, and how tax harvesting works.

paragraphs: A **capital gain** is the profit when you sell an investment for more than you paid. You're only taxed when you **sell** (realise the gain) — unrealised gains while you hold are not taxed. How much tax depends on **what** you sold and **how long** you held it.
For **equity** (listed shares and equity mutual funds), the holding-period line is **12 months**, and the rules were overhauled in the July 2024 Budget.

blocks.title: Equity capital gains — current rules (FY 2025-26)
rows: First ₹1.25 lakh of LTCG per year is tax-free
blocks.caption: STCG rate rose from 15% to 20% and LTCG from 10% to 12.5% in the July 2024 Budget; the LTCG annual exemption is ₹1.25 lakh.

blocks.title: Why this rewards patience
blocks.text: Hold equity over 12 months and your gains are taxed at 12.5% with ₹1.25 lakh tax-free; sell within 12 months and you pay 20% on every rupee of gain. The tax code literally pays you to be a long-term investor — which aligns perfectly with the buy-and-hold, goal-based approach in this course.

sections.title: A quick note on debt funds

paragraphs: The rules differ by asset. For **debt mutual funds bought after 1 April 2023**, there's no special long-term treatment — gains are added to your income and taxed at your **slab rate** regardless of holding period. So a high earner pays up to 30% on debt-fund gains, while equity gets the gentler 12.5% long-term rate.
This is a key reason equity (via index funds) is so tax-efficient for long-term wealth, and why the asset you choose interacts with the tax you'll eventually pay.

blocks.text: Aarav, currently below the tax limit, pays little or nothing on any of this today. But knowing the rules now means his future self structures holdings tax-efficiently from the start — holding equity long-term, and not parking large sums in debt funds once he's in a high slab.

sections.title: Tax harvesting: the ₹1.25 lakh annual freebie

paragraphs: Here's the insider move. Because the **first ₹1.25 lakh of LTCG each financial year is tax-free**, you can deliberately **sell** enough long-term equity to realise gains up to ₹1.25 lakh, pay zero tax on it, and immediately **rebuy** the same fund. This 'resets' your purchase price (cost basis) higher, so future gains are measured from a higher base — shrinking the taxable gain when you eventually sell for real. This is **LTCG harvesting**.

items.title: Check your unrealised LTCG
items.detail: Near year-end, see how much long-term gain (units held >12 months) you're sitting on.

items.title: Sell up to ₹1.25 lakh of gains
items.detail: Redeem enough units that the realised long-term gain is around ₹1.25 lakh — the tax-free ceiling. Tax on this: ₹0.

items.title: Rebuy the same fund
items.detail: Reinvest immediately. Your holding is restored, but your cost basis is now higher by the harvested amount.

items.title: Repeat every year
items.detail: Done annually, you keep 'using up' the ₹1.25 lakh exemption you'd otherwise waste, permanently lowering the tax due when you finally sell for a goal.

blocks.title: What harvesting can save
blocks.expression: Harvested gain × LTCG rate = tax avoided on that slice
blocks.result: By resetting the basis on ₹1.25 lakh of gains, you avoid paying 12.5% on that slice later — about **₹15,625 of tax saved per year of harvesting**, compounding into a meaningful sum over a long horizon.

blocks.title: The fine print
blocks.text: Watch three things: (1) exit loads and bid-ask/NAV timing — sell/rebuy only where costs are negligible (most index funds are fine); (2) don't trigger STCG by accidentally selling units held <12 months; (3) keep the gain at or just under ₹1.25 lakh so it stays tax-free. Also, the related move 'tax-loss harvesting' means booking losses to offset other gains — useful, but don't sell good investments purely to manufacture a loss.

cheatsheet: You're taxed on capital gains only when you SELL; unrealised gains aren't taxed.
Equity held <12 months = STCG at 20%; held ≥12 months = LTCG at 12.5%, with the first ₹1.25 lakh/year tax-free.
STCG rose to 20% and LTCG to 12.5% in the July 2024 Budget; equity LTCG has no indexation.
Debt funds bought after 1 Apr 2023 are taxed at your slab rate regardless of holding period.
The tax code rewards patience — long-term equity is taxed far more gently than short-term.
Tax harvesting: each year sell ~₹1.25 lakh of LTCG (tax-free) and rebuy to reset cost basis, saving ~₹15,625/yr in future tax.

questions.prompt: Aarav (future self) bought an index fund and is up ₹80,000 after 10 months. He's tempted to sell and 'book the profit'. What's the tax cost of selling now vs waiting two more months?
questions.hint: Where's the 12-month line, and what changes when you cross it?
answer: Selling now (held <12 months) makes the ₹80,000 a **short-term** gain taxed at 20% = ₹16,000 tax. Waiting just two more months crosses the 12-month line, making it a **long-term** gain — and since ₹80,000 is under the ₹1.25 lakh annual LTCG exemption, the tax would be **₹0**.

So impatience here costs ₹16,000 on the same profit. Unless he urgently needs the money, holding past 12 months is dramatically more tax-efficient. This is the tax code rewarding long-term behaviour — exactly what buy-and-hold investing is built around.
keyPoints: ≥12 months = LTCG, and ₹80k is under ₹1.25L exemption → ₹0

questions.prompt: Explain tax harvesting in your own words, and why selling-then-immediately-rebuying isn't a pointless round trip.
questions.hint: What happens to your cost basis after the rebuy?
answer: Tax harvesting uses the ₹1.25 lakh annual LTCG exemption that would otherwise go to waste. Each year you sell enough long-held equity to realise about ₹1.25 lakh of gains — taxed at ₹0 because it's within the exemption — then immediately rebuy the same fund.

It isn't pointless because the rebuy **resets your cost basis higher**: future gains are now measured from that higher purchase price, so when you finally sell for a real goal, the taxable gain (and thus the 12.5% tax) is smaller. You're effectively converting ₹1.25 lakh of would-be-taxable gain into tax-free gain every year, saving ~₹15,625 annually that compounds over time. The catch is to keep costs/loads negligible and avoid accidentally booking short-term gains.
keyPoints: Rebuy raises cost basis → smaller future taxable gain
Mind exit loads and the 12-month line
